details:
**Polyphemus and the curse on Odysseus**
Poseidon's son Polyphemus, a Cyclops born to the nymph Thoosa, was blinded by Odysseus, who had told him his name was "Nobody." Polyphemus prayed to his father for revenge, and Poseidon became the main adversary of the Odyssey, delaying Odysseus's return home for years; he also turned the ship of the Phaeacians to stone after they carried Odysseus back to Ithaca.

**Contest with Athena for Athens (saltwater spring vs. olive tree)**
Poseidon and Athena competed to become patron of Athens. Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident to create a saltwater spring (sometimes called the Erechtheis), but Athena's gift of the olive tree was judged better; in anger Poseidon flooded the Attic plain. Poseidon was also worshipped at Athens alongside, and identified with, the king Erechtheus.

**Medusa in Athena's temple (Pegasus and Chrysaor)**
In Ovid's version, Poseidon raped (or seduced) Medusa in Athena's temple, and Athena punished Medusa by turning her into a snake-haired Gorgon. When Perseus later beheaded Medusa, Poseidon's children by her, the winged horse Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor, sprang from her neck.

**Trident and earthquakes ("Earth-Shaker")**
Poseidon's signature weapon is the three-pronged trident, with which he strikes the ground to cause earthquakes and stirs up storms at sea. His common epithet is "Earth-Shaker" (Ennosigaios), and he is the Greek god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses, equivalent to the Roman Neptune.

**Walls of Troy and King Laomedon**
As punishment from Zeus, Poseidon and his nephew Apollo served the Trojan king Laomedon, and Poseidon built the walls of Troy. When Laomedon refused to pay them, Poseidon sent a sea monster to ravage Troy, which Heracles later killed; this grudge helps explain Poseidon's support of the Greeks in the Trojan War.

**Amphitrite and Triton**
Poseidon's wife was the Nereid Amphitrite, who at first fled from him until a dolphin found her and brought her back to be his bride. Their son Triton is a merman who blows a conch shell. In one story, Amphitrite turned Poseidon's lover Scylla into a horrible sea monster out of jealousy.

**Demeter, the stallion, and Arion**
While searching for Persephone, Demeter turned into a mare to escape Poseidon, but he changed into a stallion and mated with her. Their offspring were Arion, a swift immortal horse that could speak (later given to Adrastus), and the goddess Despoina.

**Creator and patron of horses**
Horses were sacred to Poseidon, who is said to have created the first horse (in one version, when Demeter asked him for the most beautiful animal). He rides a chariot pulled by hippocamps (sea-horses), and he gave the immortal horses Balius and Xanthus to Peleus as a wedding gift.

**Caenis transformed into Caeneus**
Poseidon raped the Lapith woman Caenis and then offered her any wish; she asked to become a man so she could never be violated again. Poseidon made her the man Caeneus with impenetrable skin, and Caeneus was later crushed into the earth with fir trees and stones by the centaurs.

**Pasiphae and the Cretan Bull**
Poseidon sent a magnificent white bull from the sea to King Minos of Crete, expecting it to be sacrificed to him. When Minos kept it instead, Poseidon made Minos's wife Pasiphae lust after the bull, and their union produced the Minotaur.

**Tyro and Enipeus (Pelias and Neleus)**
Poseidon disguised himself as the river god Enipeus, whom Tyro loved, in order to seduce her. Tyro bore him the twins Pelias (later the king who sent Jason after the Golden Fleece) and Neleus (father of Nestor of Pylos).

**The Aloadae (Otus and Ephialtes)**
Poseidon's giant twin sons by Iphimedia, who had longed for him to father her children. The Aloadae tried to storm Olympus by piling mountains on one another; Artemis, in the form of a deer, darted between them, and they killed each other with their spears trying to hit her.

**Theseus and Aethra**
Aethra slept with both the Athenian king Aegeus and Poseidon on the same night, so the hero Theseus is often called a son of Poseidon. Poseidon is also named as the father of other heroes and figures, including Bellerophon and the bandit Sinis, whom Theseus killed.

**Laocoon and the serpents**
When the Trojan priest Laocoon warned against bringing the Trojan Horse into the city, two huge sea serpents emerged from the sea and killed him and his sons. Some accounts attribute these serpents to Poseidon.

**Mestra's shapeshifting**
Poseidon, her lover, gave Mestra, the daughter of Erysichthon, the power to change her shape. Her father repeatedly sold her into marriage to pay for food for his insatiable hunger, and she escaped each time by transforming.
